note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Why does a job with many brazed joints have a written procedure that every brazer must follow?
options: So the job needs no checking or testing at the end
So each joint is made with the same filler, flux, gap and heat
So each brazer is free to pick the filler they like best
So the brazers can work without eye protection or gloves

questions.stem: Kerry-Ann's shop must braze 500 identical small steel fittings for a customer. Which heating method is likely to give the most even results?
options: One trainee with a hand torch, judging the heat by eye each time
A soldering iron of the kind used for electronics
A large heating nozzle, moved quickly over each part
Induction or furnace heating, set up once for the batch

questions.stem: A copper line on an air-conditioning unit must hold high pressure and vibration. Which joining process is normally used?
options: Brazing with a copper-phosphorus or silver filler
Soft soldering with a tin-lead plumbing solder
Gluing with two-part epoxy and a pipe clamp
Fusion welding with a copper-coated steel filler rod

questions.stem: Each joint uses about 2 g of silver brazing alloy. How much alloy should be drawn from stores for 35 joints, adding 10% for waste?
Which control is best for keeping flux and filler fumes out of a brazer's breathing zone at a fixed bench?
options: An open door at the far end of the workshop
A pedestal fan blowing the fumes across the shop
An extraction hood placed close to the joint
A paper dust mask worn over the nose and mouth

questions.stem: A trainee finds an old, unlabelled packet of silver brazing rod. What should the team leader decide?
options: Do not use it, as it may contain cadmium
Use it, as older rods flow more easily
Use it outdoors, with no other controls
Use it, but overheat it to burn off any cadmium

questions.stem: Most brazing fluxes contain fluorides and borates. Why should a brazer wash their hands before eating?
options: Flux left on the hands will make the next joint fail
Flux on the skin attracts sparks and spatter while brazing
Washing keeps the gloves dry for the next job
Flux can irritate the skin and is harmful if swallowed

questions.stem: Why must a closed hollow part, such as a sealed tube or a float, have a vent hole before it is brazed?
options: So the melted flux can drain out of the joint as it heats
Trapped air expands with heat and can burst it
So the filler can flow inside and fill it up
So the part cools faster once brazing stops

questions.stem: Brazing on a hotel roof in Negril is done under a hot work permit. What does a permit normally require after the brazing stops?
options: A fire watch on the area for the time the permit sets
Hosing the whole roof down with water before the team leaves
Nothing more, once the torch has been put out
Leaving the gas set lit in case of more work

questions.stem: Two hours after brazing brass parts, a trainee feels shivery with aching muscles, like flu. What should the supervisor do?
options: Send him back to work, as it will pass by itself
Give him milk to drink and tell him to carry on brazing
Get medical advice for him and check the fume extraction
Tell him to take a cold shower and say nothing more

questions.stem: What can happen if acetylene is drawn from a cylinder too fast, for example by a large heating nozzle?
options: The oxygen hose may burst from the back pressure it causes
Acetone can be drawn out of the cylinder with the gas
The flame turns oxidising and cannot be adjusted
The cylinder pressure rises above its safe limit

questions.stem: You are checking a trainee's oxy-acetylene set-up before brazing. Which of these must be put right before the torch is lit?
options: The hoses are coiled neatly on the trolley hook
Both cylinders are chained upright to the cylinder trolley
A bottle of leak-test solution is beside the set
There is no flashback arrestor on the fuel regulator

questions.stem: Why is oxy-acetylene often chosen over air-propane for brazing a large, heavy steel part?
options: It gives a hotter, more concentrated flame
It uses less gas and costs less to run
It gives off no fumes, so no extraction is needed
It needs no flux on steel at any thickness

questions.stem: After the torch valve is closed, the regulator's working gauge keeps slowly rising. What does this show?
options: The cylinder is nearly empty and must be changed soon
The gauge is working normally as the gas warms
The regulator seat is leaking, so take it out of use
The hose is too long for the working pressure

questions.stem: Which filler can join copper to copper without any flux?
options: A silver alloy that contains cadmium
A copper-phosphorus brazing alloy
A 60/40 brass (bronze) rod
An aluminium-silicon brazing rod

questions.stem: Why must copper-phosphorus fillers not be used to braze steel?
options: They melt at a higher heat than steel does
They turn the steel soft and bendable
They cannot be fed by hand as a rod
They form brittle compounds at the joint

questions.stem: A filler's data sheet gives a solidus of 620 °C and a liquidus of 660 °C. What does the liquidus tell you?
options: The temperature at which the filler is fully liquid
The temperature at which the filler starts to melt
The temperature at which the flux stops working
The highest temperature the parent metal can safely take

questions.stem: Why might a filler with a wide melting range (a big gap between solidus and liquidus) be chosen for a joint?
options: It runs faster and further into a very fine, tight gap
It needs no flux on any metal
It is sluggish and can bridge a wider, uneven gap
It melts at a lower heat than any other filler

questions.stem: A wide-range filler is heated very slowly. Part of it melts and runs away, leaving a lumpy, higher-melting part behind. What is this called?
options: Wetting
Erosion
Capillary flow
Liquation

questions.stem: Which filler is generally the best choice for brazing stainless steel parts on food equipment?
options: A copper-phosphorus alloy, used without any flux
A cadmium-free silver alloy suited to stainless
A tin-lead soft solder with a resin flux
Any silver alloy, as long as it is cheap

questions.stem: Why is a black, high-temperature flux sometimes chosen instead of the usual white silver brazing flux?
options: It stays active longer, for big parts or stainless
It is easier to wash off with cold water
It lets the brazer use any filler on any metal
It turns clear at a lower heat, so less gas is used

questions.stem: Why should flux be put on both parts of a joint and a little beyond the joint area?
options: So that less filler metal is needed for the job
So the flux can act as the filler in small gaps
So oxide cannot form where the filler must wet
So the parts do not need to be cleaned first

questions.stem: How should a tub of brazing flux paste be stored in the workshop?
options: Open, so it stays soft and ready to use
Lid on, labelled, as its safety data sheet says
Next to the food in the kitchen fridge
On the hot brazing bench, so it is warm when needed

questions.stem: Unless the filler maker says otherwise, which joint clearance is generally used for silver brazing a close-fitting socket?
options: About 0.5–1.0 mm
About 2–3 mm
No gap at all: a tight press fit
About 0.05–0.15 mm

questions.stem: A copper pin is to be brazed inside a steel ring. Copper expands more than steel when heated. What happens to the gap as the joint heats up?
options: It closes up, so the cold gap must be a little larger
It opens up, so the cold gap must be a tight fit
It stays exactly the same, as both metals are heated together
It opens up so far that no filler can fill it

questions.stem: A common rule makes the overlap of a brazed lap joint three times the thickness of the thinner part. What overlap is needed to braze 1.5 mm sheet to 3 mm plate?
options: 3 mm
9 mm
4.5 mm
1.5 mm

questions.stem: A 15 mm copper tube goes 12 mm deep into a fitting. Using area = π × diameter × depth, about what is the brazed area?
options: 180 mm²
565 mm²
1 130 mm²
47 mm²

questions.stem: Why is a plain butt joint in thin sheet a poor choice for brazing when the joint must be strong?
options: Butt joints cannot be cleaned before brazing
Butt joints need far more flux than lap joints
The filler cannot melt in a butt joint
The brazed area is very small, so it is weak

questions.stem: Why should a brazed lap joint be designed so that the load acts along the joint (shear) and does not peel it apart?
options: Brazed joints are weak in shear but strong in peel
Shear loads stop the flux from washing out
Brazed laps are strong in shear but weak in peel
Peeling loads make the joint expand when hot

questions.stem: A steel part is both greasy and rusty. In which order should it be cleaned before brazing?
options: Remove the grease first, then clean off the rust
Grind off the rust first, then wipe off the grease
Flux it heavily, so no cleaning is needed
Heat it red hot to burn off both, then braze

questions.stem: Why should parts be brazed soon after they are cleaned?
options: So the cleaning solvent can act as a flux
So new oxide and dirt do not have time to form
So the parts are still warm from the cleaning
So the clean parts do not need flux

questions.stem: Why should a brazing jig be light and touch the parts at only a few small points?
options: So the filler can also braze the jig to the part
So that the jig can be made of plastic
So that the parts can move about while heated
A heavy jig draws heat away from the joint

questions.stem: Why is a wet cloth or heat-sink paste sometimes put on a part next to the joint before brazing?
options: To keep the flux from drying out too soon
To make the filler flow away from the joint
To stop heat damaging a nearby seal or valve seat
To cool the joint so the filler sets more quickly

questions.stem: A brazer melts the rod in the flame and drips it onto the joint to save time. Why is this poor practice?
options: The joint is not hot enough for the filler to wet it
It wastes some gas, but the joint will be just as sound
It is fine, as long as the flux is fresh
The rod will catch fire in the flame

questions.stem: When braze welding with brass rod, why is a slightly oxidising flame often used?
options: It makes the flame softer, quieter and easier to hold
It cuts down the zinc fumes given off by the brass
It stops the steel from needing any cleaning
It lets the brazer work without any flux

questions.stem: When a test joint is cut open, the filler is seen to have eaten into the parent metal (erosion). Which change will most help to prevent this?
options: Use a bigger torch nozzle and heat for longer
Feed far more filler into the joint than before
Leave out the flux so the filler flows less
Heat for less time and not above what is needed

questions.stem: At the end of a group's brazing session, what should the team leader check before the group leaves?
options: Valves closed, hoses bled, hot parts marked, area checked
That the torch is left lit and ready for the next class
That the hoses are left holding full gas pressure overnight
That the flux tubs are left open to stay soft

questions.stem: A brazed lap test piece is clamped in a vice and the top sheet is levered and rolled back with pliers. What does this test show?
options: The hardness and the colour of the filler metal
Whether the parts were cut to the right length
How much of the overlap the filler wetted
How hot the joint got while brazing

questions.stem: Why is one sample joint from a batch sometimes cut through and examined?
options: To make the batch lighter for delivery
To see voids and fill inside the joint
To check the colour of the flux used
To find out how much the gas cost

questions.stem: A brazed copper pipe assembly is to be pressure tested. Why is water usually used rather than compressed air?
options: Water finds leaks faster than air does
Air would corrode the brazed joints
Water cools the joints while testing
A burst is far less violent with water

questions.stem: Sections show flux trapped in the middle of several socket joints. Which is a likely cause?
options: Filler was fed from both ends, trapping the flux
The parts were cleaned far too well before brazing
The joint was left to cool without moving it
The filler used had too much silver in it

questions.stem: Several steel-to-copper joints crack as they cool. The parts were a tight press fit. What is the most likely cause?
options: The filler had far too much silver for the job
The flux was put on too thinly at the joint
Different expansion of the two metals
The parts were cooled slowly in still air

questions.stem: A brass braze weld has many small gas holes, and white fumes came off while it was made. What is the most likely cause?
options: The filler rod was far too thin for the joint
Overheating made the zinc in the brass boil
The steel was cleaned to bright metal
The flame was too small and too cool

questions.stem: A trainee in your team starts brazing without goggles, 'just for one quick joint'. What should you do as the leader?
options: Let him finish, then talk to him at the end of the day
Say nothing, as one quick joint is low risk
Write it in the report but let the work go on
Stop the work at once until he wears the right goggles

questions.stem: At the end of a batch, three joints failed the leak test. Which is the best content for your report?
options: Which joints failed, the test, the likely cause and the repair
Only the number of joints that passed the test
The names of the trainees, so they can be punished
Nothing, if the joints are repaired before delivery

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: In production, what is the name for a ring or shaped piece of filler metal placed on the joint before it is heated?
What is the name for the mild acid bath used to remove oxide and flux from parts after brazing?
Which precious metal is added to some copper-phosphorus fillers to make them less brittle and help them flow?
Which highly toxic gas can form when welding near chlorinated degreasing solvents?
What is the name for the small, smooth curve of filler that shows at the edge of a good brazed joint?
What is the name of the heat-resistant blocks that work is laid on while it is brazed?
A brazing alloy contains 55% silver. How many grams of silver are in a 50 g coil of it?
A regulator gauge reads 1.5 bar. What is this pressure in kilopascals (kPa)?
What is the first inspection made on every brazed joint, using the eyes, good light and perhaps a magnifier?
What is the name of the sharp, raised edge left inside a tube after it is cut, which must be removed before brazing?
What tool cuts copper tube square, using a sharp wheel that is turned around the tube?
What is the name of the test that uses a coloured liquid and a developer to show fine cracks on the surface?
One joint uses 1.2 g of silver alloy that costs J$400 per gram. What is the cost of the alloy for one joint, in J$?
A job has 120 joints, and one brazer can make 15 good joints an hour. How many hours of brazing are needed?
Which non-flammable gas is passed through copper refrigeration pipe while it is brazed, to stop black scale forming inside?

essays.stem: You are leading a team that must silver braze 30 identical copper-to-brass joints for a customer. Explain how you would plan the job, from the drawing to the records you keep.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the drawing and the customer's order to confirm the metals, the joint type, the sizes, the number of joints and any test the customer wants. I then write or check the brazing procedure: a cadmium-free silver filler that suits copper and brass, the matching flux, the joint clearance, the flame and the heating method. I work out the materials, with about 10% extra filler for waste, and book the gas set and the fume extraction. I share out the work: who cleans and fits, who brazes and who inspects. Before production I make and test two sample joints to prove the procedure. I check the hot work area, the PPE and the fire extinguisher, and give the team a short safety talk. During the job I check joints as they are made. At the end I record the batch, the tests and results, and any repairs on the job card.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing and order: metals, joint, sizes, number of joints and tests
Sets the procedure: cadmium-free filler, flux, clearance, flame and heating method
Plans materials (with a waste allowance), equipment and who does each task
Proves the procedure on sample joints and briefs the team on safety
Inspects during the job and records tests, results and repairs

essays.stem: Explain how joint design affects the strength of a brazed joint. Include the joint type, the overlap, the clearance, and the effect of joining two metals that expand by different amounts.
essays.modelAnswer: A brazed joint is strongest when the filler is spread over a large area in a thin, even film. Lap and socket joints are best because they give a large brazed area; a plain butt joint in thin sheet has very little area and is weak. A common rule is an overlap of about three times the thickness of the thinner part. The clearance must be small and even, generally about 0.05–0.15 mm for silver alloys or the figure the filler maker gives, so that capillary action can draw the filler right through. Too tight and the filler cannot get in; too wide and capillary action fails and voids form. When two metals expand by different amounts, the gap changes as they heat. A copper part inside a steel part closes the gap, so the cold gap must be larger; the other way round, the gap opens. The joint should also be loaded in shear, not peel.
markingPoints: Lap or socket joints give a large brazed area; plain butt joints are weak
Overlap of about three times the thinner part
Small, even clearance (about 0.05–0.15 mm or the maker's figure) so capillary flow works; effect of too tight or too wide
Different expansion changes the gap at brazing heat, so the cold gap is set to suit
Joint loaded in shear, not peel

essays.stem: A customer needs stainless steel joined to copper on a food-processing machine. Explain how you would choose the filler metal, the flux and the heating method, giving your reasons.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the drawing, any customer specification and how the part will be used: food contact, cleaning chemicals, temperature and pressure. For stainless steel to copper I would choose a cadmium-free silver brazing alloy that the maker lists as suitable for stainless steel, because cadmium is toxic and must never be near food. A copper-phosphorus filler cannot be used, because it forms brittle compounds on the stainless steel. Stainless steel has a tough oxide skin, so I would use the flux the filler maker matches to stainless steel, often a high-temperature (black) flux that stays active longer. For heating I would use a torch with a neutral or slightly reducing flame, big enough to heat the joint quickly and evenly, because long heating uses up the flux and discolours the stainless. The heavier part gets more of the heat. After brazing, all the flux is removed and the joint is inspected before the machine is used. I follow the maker's instructions for the filler and flux.
markingPoints: Checks the drawing, specification and service conditions (food contact)
Cadmium-free silver alloy suited to stainless steel; no copper-phosphorus on stainless (brittle)
Flux matched to stainless steel, often high-temperature, because of the tough oxide
Heating chosen for quick, even heat; heavier part heated more
Removes all flux and inspects; follows the maker's instructions

essays.stem: As the person in charge of a brazing area, explain how you would control the fume, fire and gas hazards before, during and after the work.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work I check the job for any metal or coating that gives toxic fumes, such as cadmium, zinc or paint, and I make sure only cadmium-free fillers are issued. I set up an extraction hood close to the joint and check that it works. I clear or cover anything that can burn, put a suitable extinguisher at hand, and get a hot work permit where the site needs one. I check the gas set: cylinders upright and chained, flashback arrestors fitted, hoses sound and every joint leak tested with leak-test solution. Everyone wears tinted goggles (about shade 3–5), leather gloves and flame-resistant clothing. During the work I make sure the extraction is used and heads are kept out of the fumes, and I stop any unsafe act at once. After the work I check that the gas is shut down and the hoses bled, hot parts are marked, flux tubs are closed, and the area is watched for fire for the time the permit or the Centre's rules set.
markingPoints: Fume: cadmium-free fillers, coatings checked, extraction close to the joint
Fire: combustibles cleared, extinguisher, hot work permit, fire watch afterwards
Gas: cylinders secured, arrestors fitted, hoses checked and leak tested
PPE: tinted goggles (about shade 3–5), leather gloves, flame-resistant clothing
Supervises during and after: stops unsafe acts, shuts down, marks hot parts

essays.stem: Describe the inspection and tests you would carry out on a brazed copper pipe assembly before it is handed over, and how you would record the results.
essays.modelAnswer: When the assembly is cool and the flux has been washed off, I make a visual inspection of every joint in good light. I look for a full, smooth fillet all round each joint, with no gaps, cracks, pinholes, burnt flux or erosion, and no filler run down the pipe. I check the sizes and positions against the drawing. Then I do a pressure test. I fill the assembly with water, bleed out the air, and use a hand test pump and a checked gauge to raise it to the test pressure given in the specification or by the supervisor. I hold the pressure for the set time, look at every joint for drips and watch the gauge for any drop. Water is used because a failure is far less violent than with air. Any failed joint is marked, repaired and tested again. I record the job number, the joints checked, the test pressure, the hold time, the gauge used, the results, any repairs, the date and my name, and I sign the record.
markingPoints: Flux washed off, then a visual inspection of every joint (fillet, gaps, cracks, pinholes, burnt flux)
Sizes and positions checked against the drawing
Water pressure test at the specified pressure and hold time, watching joints and gauge
Failed joints marked, repaired and tested again
Records job, test pressure, hold time, results and repairs, signed and dated

essays.stem: Sections cut from three sample joints show (1) voids, (2) flux trapped in the joint and (3) erosion of the parent metal. For each fault, explain a likely cause and what you would change in the procedure.
essays.modelAnswer: (1) Voids are empty spaces where the filler did not fill the joint. Likely causes are dirty or oxidised surfaces, a gap that is too wide or uneven, or uneven heating so that parts of the joint were not hot enough. I would improve the cleaning, check the clearance with the parts fitted, and heat the whole joint evenly before feeding the filler. (2) Trapped flux usually comes from feeding filler from both sides, which shuts the flux in the middle, or from too much flux or uneven heat. I would feed the filler from one side only, so that it pushes the flux out ahead of it, and use a thin, even coat of flux. (3) Erosion is the filler dissolving the parent metal. It comes from overheating, heating for too long, or too much filler. I would use a smaller flame, heat for no longer than needed, and control the amount of filler, for example with preforms. After the changes, I would make and section new sample joints to prove the procedure.
markingPoints: Voids: dirty surface, wrong gap or uneven heat, with a matching change
Trapped flux: filler fed from both sides or too much flux; feed from one side, thin coat
Erosion: overheating, long heating or excess filler; less heat and time, control the filler
Proves the changed procedure with new sample joints

essays.stem: A new trainee in your team keeps making joints where the filler balls up on the surface and does not run in. Explain how you would find the cause and coach the trainee to correct it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first watch the trainee make a joint without stepping in, and look at the parts and the equipment. Filler that balls up usually means the parent metal is not hot enough, or the surface is dirty or oxidised so the filler cannot wet it. Other causes are the wrong flux, flux that has burnt out from heating too long, or melting the rod in the flame instead of on the hot joint. I would check that the parts are cleaned to bright metal and fluxed straight away, that the flux matches the filler and the metal, and that the flame size suits the part. Then I would show the trainee how to heat the whole joint evenly, watch the flux turn clear, and touch the rod to the joint away from the flame so that the hot metal melts it. The trainee would then make sample joints while I watch, and we would peel or cut one open to check the fill. I would praise good joints and record the coaching.
markingPoints: Watches the trainee work and checks the parts and set-up before deciding
Names likely causes: joint not hot enough, dirty surface, wrong or burnt flux, rod melted in the flame
Corrects the cleaning, the flux choice and the flame size
Shows the right method: even heat, flux turns clear, rod onto the hot joint
Trainee practises, sample joints are tested, and the coaching is recorded

essays.stem: Compare torch, induction and furnace brazing. Say which you would choose for a one-off repair and for a run of 500 identical parts, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: Torch brazing uses a hand-held oxy-fuel or air-fuel flame. It needs little set-up and the equipment can be carried to the job, so it suits repairs and one-off work, but the quality depends on the brazer's skill and it is slow for large numbers. Induction brazing heats the joint with a copper coil carrying a high-frequency current. It heats only the joint area, quickly and the same way each time, but each coil must be made to suit the part, so it is best for runs of the same part. Furnace brazing heats whole assemblies in a controlled furnace, often with preforms of filler and sometimes in a protective gas so that no flux is needed. It is good for many parts at once and for joints that are hard to reach, but the equipment is costly and the whole part gets hot. For a one-off repair I would use a torch, because it is quick to set up and portable. For 500 identical parts I would choose induction or furnace brazing, because the results are even and repeatable and the cost per part is lower.
markingPoints: Torch: portable, little set-up, depends on skill, slow for large numbers
Induction: fast heating of the joint only, repeatable, coil made for the part
Furnace: many parts at once, controlled atmosphere, costly, whole part heated
One-off repair: torch, with a reason
500 parts: induction or furnace, with a reason

essays.stem: Explain why a brazing procedure is tried on sample joints before production starts, and list what a written brazing procedure should include.
essays.modelAnswer: A procedure is tried on sample joints to prove that the filler, flux, clearance and heating will give sound joints on the real parts before time and material are spent on production. The sample joints are inspected and then tested, for example by peel tests or by cutting them open, to check that the filler has filled the joint with no voids, trapped flux or erosion. If they fail, the procedure is changed and tried again. Once it is proven, every brazer can make the joint the same way, and the results can be shown to the customer or the inspector. A written procedure should include: the parent metals and their thickness or size; the joint type, overlap and clearance; the filler metal and its form; the flux; the cleaning method; the heating method, fuel gas, nozzle and flame; how the filler is fed; any jig or support; the cleaning after brazing; and the inspection and tests, with what counts as a pass. It also has a number, a date and the name of the person who approved it.
markingPoints: Proves the procedure gives sound joints before production; samples tested by peel or section
Procedure changed and tried again if samples fail; a proven procedure gives repeatable joints and evidence
Includes the metals, joint type, overlap and clearance
Includes the filler, flux, cleaning, heating method and flame
Includes cleaning after brazing, inspection and test criteria, and approval

essays.stem: A brazed joint on an air-conditioning copper line at a hotel in Ocho Rios leaked after one week in use. Explain how you would investigate the failure and what your written report should contain.
essays.modelAnswer: First the line must be made safe: the system is isolated and the refrigerant is recovered by a qualified technician. I never heat a line that still holds refrigerant or pressure. I look at the joint and the area around it: is the leak in the joint, beside it, or in a crack in the pipe? I check for vibration, poor support or rubbing that could have stressed the joint. I find the job records to see who made the joint, which filler and procedure were used, and whether it was pressure tested. If the joint is cut out, I look at the cut faces for voids, poor fill, erosion or cracks. From this I decide the likely cause and the repair, such as remaking the joint with better cleaning and heating and adding a pipe clip. My report gives the date, the place and the job number, what was found, photos, the likely cause, the repair, the test results after the repair, and what will change to stop it happening again. I sign and date it.
markingPoints: Makes it safe: system isolated, refrigerant recovered by a qualified person, no pressure in the line
Examines the joint and its surroundings (vibration, support, cracks) and checks the job records
Examines the joint for voids, poor fill, erosion or cracks and decides the cause
Repairs and tests again
Report: details, findings, photos, cause, repair, test results and prevention, signed and dated

practical1.title: Planning, silver brazing and pressure testing a copper manifold to a written procedure
practical1.brief: Your group is asked to make a small copper manifold for a customer, to the assessor's drawing: a run of 22 mm copper tube with three 22 mm × 15 mm reducing tees, a 15 mm stub and end cap on each branch, an end cap at one end and a test-pump connector at the other. First, as a group, write a one-page brazing procedure for the job (filler, flux, clearance, cleaning, heating, the order of the joints, and the test) and a short risk assessment for the hot work. One member leads the planning and the safety check before lighting; a different member leads the testing. Every member cuts, cleans, fits, fluxes and brazes at least two joints while the assessor watches, and checks and records another member's joints. When the manifold is cool and washed, the group carries out a water pressure test with a hand test pump and gauge, to the pressure and hold time the assessor sets, and records the result on a test sheet. Any leaking joint is marked, repaired and tested again. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the procedure, risk assessment, test sheet and photos once for the whole group, when the area is clean and the gas is shut down.
materials: 22 mm copper tube (about 1 m) and 15 mm copper tube (about 0.5 m)
Three 22 mm × 15 mm copper reducing tees, three 15 mm end caps, one 22 mm end cap and a connector for the test pump
Cadmium-free silver brazing alloy and the matching flux (or the filler the procedure names)
Tube cutter, deburring tool, emery cloth and fitting brushes
Oxy-acetylene or air-propane set with flashback arrestors, and a spark lighter
Extraction hood, firebricks, fire extinguisher and tongs
Hand water test pump with a checked pressure gauge
Procedure sheet, risk assessment form and test sheet

practical2.title: Silver brazing dissimilar-metal lap joints, with peel and section tests and a written test report
practical2.brief: Your group will test a brazing procedure for joining mild steel to copper and mild steel to brass, and write a short report on the results. Plan the test with the assessor. Each member makes two lap joints from strips about 100 mm × 25 mm: 1.5 mm mild steel to 1.5 mm copper, and 1.5 mm mild steel to 1.5 mm brass, using a cadmium-free silver alloy and the matching flux. Half of the group uses an overlap of three times the thickness (4.5 mm) and the other half uses the overlap the assessor sets, so the results can be compared. Label every test piece with the member's initials and the overlap. When the pieces are cool and cleaned, peel test one joint from each member in the vice, and saw the other across, file the cut face smooth and look at it with a magnifier. Estimate how much of each overlap is filled, record every result in a table, and write a one-page report giving the results, the faults found and their likely causes, and the procedure the group recommends. Every member brazes, tests and writes part of the report. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: 1.5 mm mild steel, copper and brass strips, about 100 mm × 25 mm (two steel strips, one copper and one brass for each member)
Cadmium-free silver brazing alloy suitable for steel, copper and brass, and the matching flux
Oxy-acetylene or air-propane set with flashback arrestors, and a spark lighter
Firebricks, small clamps or a simple jig, tongs and extraction
Bench vice, large pliers, hacksaw, magnifier and steel rule
Hot water and a scrubbing brush for removing flux
Marker or letter punches, a results table and a report sheet
